name: Cryptography Basics
author: Recurse
subject: security
description: Encryption, hashing, password storage, signatures, certificates and TLS, and the mistakes that break them.

lesson.intro: Cryptography is the math that keeps data secret, detects tampering and proves who you are talking to. You will almost never implement it yourself, but you will choose and use it constantly. This lesson explains what each building block guarantees, how they fit together in TLS, and the mistakes that quietly undo them.

sections.title: Symmetric and asymmetric encryption
sections.body:
Encryption turns readable plaintext into ciphertext that only someone with the right key can turn back.

Symmetric encryption uses one shared secret key for both encrypting and decrypting. It is fast enough for gigabytes of data. AES (Advanced Encryption Standard) is the standard choice, used in an authenticated mode such as AES-GCM, which also detects any change to the ciphertext. ChaCha20-Poly1305 is a common alternative.

The catch is key distribution: both sides need the same key, and you cannot simply send it over the network you are trying to protect.

Asymmetric (public-key) encryption uses a key pair:

- The public key can be shared with anyone. What it encrypts, only the matching private key can decrypt.
- The private key never leaves its owner.
- RSA and elliptic-curve cryptography are the common families.

Asymmetric operations are much slower, so they are used for small jobs: agreeing on keys and making signatures. Real systems are hybrid. Public-key cryptography sets up a shared symmetric key, then AES or ChaCha20 encrypts the actual data. TLS, SSH and Signal all work this way.
sections.code:
import os
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.ciphers.aead import AESGCM

key = AESGCM.generate_key(bit_length=256)   # the shared secret
aesgcm = AESGCM(key)
nonce = os.urandom(12)                       # never reuse a nonce with the same key

ct = aesgcm.encrypt(nonce, b"attack at dawn", None)
print(aesgcm.decrypt(nonce, ct, None))       # b'attack at dawn'
sections.tip: Authenticated modes like GCM raise an error on decrypt if even one bit of the ciphertext was changed.

check.question: Which problem does asymmetric encryption solve that symmetric encryption alone does not?
choices: Encrypting large files and backups much more quickly
Making ciphertext shorter than plaintext
Talking privately with someone you never shared a key with
Detecting accidental changes to stored files
check.explanation: With a public key, anyone can encrypt to you without a shared secret arranged in advance. Symmetric ciphers are the fast ones, so bulk encryption is their job, not asymmetric encryption's.

sections.title: Hash functions
sections.body:
A cryptographic hash function turns any input into a fixed-size fingerprint. SHA-256 always outputs 256 bits, written as 64 hex characters, whether the input is one byte or a whole movie.

- Deterministic: the same input always gives the same hash.
- One-way (preimage resistance): given a hash, you cannot find an input that produces it, except by guessing.
- Collision resistance: it is infeasible to find any two different inputs with the same hash.
- Avalanche effect: changing one bit of input changes about half the output bits, so similar inputs give unrelated hashes.

A hash has no key and cannot be decrypted. Its main job is integrity: a publisher lists a file's hash, and anyone can confirm their download matches. A matching hash says the file is unchanged; it says nothing about whether the file is safe, since anyone can hash a malicious file.

MD5 and SHA-1 are broken: researchers can produce collisions, so do not use them for security. SHA-256, SHA-3 and BLAKE2 are fine.

HMAC combines a hash with a secret key, so only someone who holds the key can produce a valid tag. It protects messages such as API requests and webhooks from tampering.
sections.tip: One changed letter, a completely different hash: that is the avalanche effect.

check.question: Two files have different SHA-256 hashes. What can you conclude?
choices: Their contents are different
One of them is corrupted
They have different file names
One of them is encrypted
check.explanation: Hashing is deterministic, so identical contents always give identical hashes. Different hashes mean the bytes differ, but not which one is right; and names are not part of the hash.

sections.title: Storing passwords: salts and slow hashes
sections.body:
General-purpose hashes like SHA-256 are designed to be fast. That is a problem for passwords. If a database leaks, attackers use GPUs to hash billions of guesses per second and compare them with the stolen hashes. Most human-chosen passwords fall quickly.

Two defenses work together:

- A salt is a random value, unique to each user, stored next to the hash and mixed into it. Two users with the same password get different hashes, and precomputed lookup tables (rainbow tables) become useless because each salt would need its own table. A salt is not a secret.
- A slow password hash makes every guess expensive. bcrypt has a cost factor, and each +1 doubles the work. Argon2id, winner of the 2015 Password Hashing Competition, is also memory-hard, which blunts GPUs and custom hardware. scrypt is a similar older option.

Tune the cost so one hash takes a noticeable fraction of a second on your server. One login never feels it, but an attacker trying a billion guesses pays that price a billion times.

Good libraries handle the salt for you. A bcrypt hash string contains the algorithm version, the cost and the salt, so you store just that one string and pass it back when checking.
sections.code:
import bcrypt

stored = bcrypt.hashpw(b"correct horse battery staple", bcrypt.gensalt(rounds=12))
print(stored)
# b'$2b$12$6jZ8u922B3FZKNPf/k4aDuhGg5L3QzleGx/Yi0aSxLRCuOj3klf2q'
#    version $2b, cost 12, then 22 characters of salt and 31 of hash

bcrypt.checkpw(b"correct horse battery staple", stored)   # True
bcrypt.checkpw(b"Tr0ub4dor&3", stored)                    # False
sections.tip: The cost factor is an exponent: cost 12 means 2^12 rounds of the expensive setup step.

check.question: Why is a deliberately slow hash a good choice for storing passwords?
choices: It produces a longer hash that is harder to read or copy
It lets the server decrypt passwords when users forget them
It removes the need to store a separate salt per user
Every attacker guess pays the delay, making mass guessing impractical
check.explanation: A legitimate user hashes once per login and never notices a short delay, but an attacker must pay it for every guess. Slow hashes still need salts, and no password hash can be decrypted.

sections.title: Signatures, certificates and the TLS trust chain
sections.body:
A digital signature uses a key pair the other way around. The signer uses their private key to sign (a hash of) a message, and anyone with the matching public key can verify it. A valid signature proves:

- Integrity: the message has not changed since it was signed.
- Authenticity: it was signed by whoever holds the private key.
- Non-repudiation: the signer cannot easily deny signing it.

A signature does not hide anything. A signed but unencrypted message is readable by anyone who sees it.

Signatures raise a question: how do you know a public key really belongs to your bank? A certificate binds a public key to a name like `www.example.com`, plus validity dates, and is signed by a certificate authority (CA).

When you connect over HTTPS, the browser checks a chain of trust:

- The server sends its leaf certificate for `www.example.com` and an intermediate CA certificate.
- The leaf is signed by the intermediate, and the intermediate is signed by a root CA.
- The root CA's certificate is already in your browser's or operating system's trust store. Trust flows down from it; a root that the server sends is not trusted just because it was sent.

The browser also checks that the name matches the site, the dates are valid, and the certificate has not been revoked. A certificate warning means one of these checks failed, which is exactly what an impersonation attack looks like.
sections.code:
Root CA certificate           self-signed, preinstalled in your trust store
   |  signs
   v
Intermediate CA certificate   sent by the server
   |  signs
   v
Leaf certificate              www.example.com, its public key, valid dates
sections.tip: Run `openssl s_client -connect example.com:443 -showcerts` to see the chain a server actually sends.

check.question: In a certificate chain, which certificate must already be in your browser or OS trust store?
choices: The leaf certificate for the site
The root CA certificate
The intermediate CA certificate
None; the server sends everything needed
check.explanation: Trust has to start somewhere the attacker cannot control, which is the preinstalled root. The server sends the leaf and intermediates, and the browser verifies each signature up to that trusted root.

sections.title: Key exchange and common mistakes
sections.body:
Key exchange solves the key distribution problem. In Diffie-Hellman, each side picks a secret number, sends a public value derived from it, and combines the other side's public value with its own secret. Both end up with the same shared secret, yet an eavesdropper who saw only the public values cannot compute it. Modern TLS uses ECDHE, the elliptic-curve version with fresh (ephemeral) keys for every connection.

- Fresh keys give forward secrecy: session keys are discarded after use, so stealing the server's private key later does not decrypt traffic someone recorded earlier.
- Plain Diffie-Hellman does not prove who is on the other end. An active man-in-the-middle could run one exchange with you and another with the server. TLS stops this by having the server sign the handshake with its certificate's private key.

In a TLS 1.3 handshake, the client and server exchange key shares, the server proves its identity with its certificate and a signature, and both derive symmetric keys that encrypt the rest of the connection.

Common mistakes that break good algorithms:

- ECB mode encrypts each 16-byte block on its own, so identical plaintext blocks give identical ciphertext blocks and patterns show through. Use an authenticated mode such as GCM.
- Reusing a nonce with the same key in GCM or CTR mode can expose plaintext and allow forgeries.
- Using `random` for tokens or keys. It is predictable; use the `secrets` module.
- Hardcoding keys in source code, where they end up in Git history.
- Rolling your own crypto. New algorithms and protocols are very hard to get right; use well-reviewed libraries. Security should depend only on keeping the key secret, never on keeping the design secret (Kerckhoffs's principle).
sections.code:
import secrets

reset_token = secrets.token_urlsafe(32)   # 32 random bytes, safe to put in a link
api_key = secrets.token_hex(32)           # 64 hex characters

# Compare secrets in constant time to avoid leaking them through timing
secrets.compare_digest(api_key, api_key)  # True
sections.tip: If you are choosing a cipher mode or padding scheme by hand, you are probably working one level too low. Prefer high-level library APIs.

check.question: A startup designs its own cipher and keeps the algorithm secret, saying that makes it safer. What is the best response?
choices: Fine, as long as the key is also long and random
Fine, since attackers cannot break an algorithm they are unable to see
Likely weaker: security should rest on the key, not a hidden design
It becomes safe if the data is encrypted with it twice
check.explanation: Secret designs get no public review and are usually broken once someone reverse-engineers them. Kerckhoffs's principle says a system should stay secure even if everything except the key is public, which is how AES is used.

keyTerms.definition: Encryption where one shared secret key both encrypts and decrypts, such as AES-GCM.
Encryption with a key pair: data encrypted with the public key can only be decrypted with the private key.
A one-way function that maps any input to a fixed-size, collision-resistant fingerprint, such as SHA-256.
A random, per-user value mixed into a password hash so identical passwords hash differently and lookup tables fail.
A value made with a private key that anyone can verify with the public key, proving integrity and authenticity.
An organization whose signature on a certificate vouches that a public key belongs to a given name.
A key exchange that lets two parties derive the same shared secret while sending only public values.
A property of using fresh key-exchange keys per session, so a later key theft cannot decrypt past traffic.

summary: Symmetric ciphers like AES are fast but need a shared key; asymmetric keys solve sharing, and real systems combine both.
Hashes are one-way, fixed-size fingerprints for integrity; they have no key and cannot be decrypted.
Store passwords with a per-user salt and a deliberately slow hash such as Argon2id or bcrypt, never a fast hash.
Signatures prove who signed and that nothing changed; certificates chain up to a root CA your device already trusts.
Use ephemeral key exchange, authenticated modes and vetted libraries; avoid ECB, nonce reuse, random for secrets and homemade crypto.
lesson.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a friend how their browser can be sure it is really talking to their bank and then set up a private connection, even though the bank and the browser have never shared a secret before.

questions.question: Bob wants anyone to be able to send him messages that only he can read. Which key do the senders encrypt with?
choices: Bob's private key
Bob's public key
Each sender's own private key
A key Bob emails to each sender
questions.explanation: Senders encrypt with Bob's public key, and only Bob's private key can decrypt the result. Bob's private key must never be shared, and emailing keys around brings back the key distribution problem.

questions.question: Why does TLS use both asymmetric and symmetric cryptography instead of just one?
questions.answer: Asymmetric cryptography solves key distribution and identity but is slow, so TLS uses it only to agree on a shared secret and to authenticate the server. The bulk data is then encrypted with a fast symmetric cipher such as AES-GCM.
questions.explanation: This hybrid design gets the best of both: public keys let strangers connect safely, and symmetric ciphers keep the connection fast.

questions.question: Which symmetric cipher is the standard choice today for encrypting bulk data? Give its three-letter acronym.
questions.explanation: AES, the Advanced Encryption Standard, is used for disk encryption, TLS, VPNs and more, usually in an authenticated mode such as GCM. RSA is asymmetric, so it is not used for bulk data.

questions.question: You download an installer, and its SHA-256 hash matches the one listed on the vendor's HTTPS download page. What does that tell you?
choices: The installer is free of malware
The installer is encrypted
The installer was signed with the vendor's private key
Your copy is identical to the file the vendor hashed
questions.explanation: A matching hash means the bytes are unchanged, so the download was not corrupted or swapped in transit. It does not prove the file is safe, and a hash is not a signature, since anyone can compute one.

questions.question: How many hexadecimal characters long is a SHA-256 digest?
questions.explanation: SHA-256 outputs 256 bits. Each hex character encodes 4 bits, so 256 / 4 = 64 characters, no matter how long the input is.

questions.question: What does it mean that a hash function is collision resistant?
choices: It is hard to find an input that produces one given hash
The hash cannot be turned back into the input by anyone without the key
It is hard to find any two different inputs that produce the same hash
Different inputs produce outputs of different lengths
questions.explanation: Collision resistance is about finding any matching pair. Finding an input for one given hash is preimage resistance, a different property. Hashes have no key, and their output length is always fixed.

questions.question: What does adding a unique salt to each password hash protect against?
choices: Precomputed lookup tables, and spotting users who share a password
Fast guessing, because each individual hash takes much longer to compute
Attackers reading the hashes out of the database
Users picking short or common passwords in the first place
questions.explanation: With a unique salt, identical passwords hash differently and a precomputed table would have to be rebuilt for every salt. Slowing each guess is the job of the cost factor in bcrypt or Argon2, not the salt.

questions.question: Complete the login check so it returns True only when the password is correct.
choices: hashpw
checkpw
gensalt
kdf
questions.explanation: checkpw re-hashes the attempt with the salt and cost stored in stored_hash and returns True or False. hashpw returns hash bytes, which are always truthy, so every login would pass.

questions.question: This app hashes passwords with a salt. What is the real weakness?
choices: The salt must be appended after the password, never before it
hexdigest() loses information; digest() is needed to keep every bit
SHA-256 is broken by collision attacks, so hashes can be forged
One shared salt plus a fast hash: equal passwords match and guessing is cheap
questions.explanation: A salt shared by every user means equal passwords still produce equal hashes and one cracking run covers everyone, and SHA-256 lets attackers try billions of guesses per second. SHA-256 is not broken; it is just too fast for passwords.

questions.question: Each +1 to bcrypt's cost factor doubles the work. If a hash takes 250 ms at cost 12, about how many milliseconds does it take at cost 14?
questions.explanation: Going from cost 12 to 14 is two doublings: 250 x 2 x 2 = 1000 ms. The same factor of 4 applies to every guess an attacker makes.

questions.question: Alice wants to sign a contract file so anyone can check it came from her. Which keys are used?
choices: Alice signs with her private key; anyone verifies with her public key
Alice signs with her public key; Bob verifies with his own private key
Alice signs with Bob's public key; Bob verifies with his private key
Alice and Bob both use one shared secret key
questions.explanation: Only Alice holds her private key, so only she can make the signature, and anyone with her public key can verify it. Encrypting with Bob's public key gives secrecy, not proof of who sent it.

questions.question: Alice digitally signs an email but does not encrypt it. Which statement is true?
choices: Only the intended recipient is able to read its contents
Nobody can read it unless they have Alice's private key
Anyone who intercepts it can read it, but edits would be detected
It can no longer be forwarded to others without breaking the signature
questions.explanation: A signature provides integrity and authenticity, not confidentiality. The content travels in the clear; any edit would make the signature check fail.

questions.question: Your browser accepts the certificate for www.example.com without a warning. Why does it trust it?
choices: The server also sent a root certificate, which the browser accepts
It chains to a root CA in the trust store, and its name and dates check out
The certificate itself is encrypted with the site's private key
The page was loaded over port 443, which is always trusted
questions.explanation: Trust starts at a root CA that is preinstalled, then each signature down the chain is verified, along with the name, dates and revocation status. A root supplied by the server proves nothing, because an attacker could send their own.

questions.question: This script talks to an internal API over HTTPS. What is the security problem?
choices: verify=False skips certificate checks, so anyone can pose as the API
HTTPS requests also need ssl=True before traffic is encrypted
verify=False only skips the hostname check; the chain is still validated
resp.json() returns encrypted data that must be decrypted first
questions.explanation: With verify=False, requests accepts any certificate, so an attacker on the network can present their own and read or alter everything. The traffic is still encrypted, but to whoever answered. Fix the trust store instead, for example by passing verify with the path to your internal CA bundle.

questions.question: Which statement about plain Diffie-Hellman key exchange is true?
choices: The shared secret is sent over the network, but encrypted
It proves the server's identity to the client on its own
It encrypts all of the application data directly
It stops eavesdroppers but not an active man-in-the-middle
questions.explanation: The secret is never sent; each side computes it from public values. Because nothing in plain Diffie-Hellman proves identity, an attacker in the middle can run separate exchanges with each side, which is why TLS adds a certificate signature.

questions.question: Why is encrypting data with AES in ECB mode a mistake?
choices: ECB only supports short 56-bit keys, which are easy to brute-force
ECB ciphertext cannot be decrypted without the plaintext
Identical plaintext blocks encrypt identically, so patterns leak
ECB is much slower than every other block cipher mode
questions.explanation: ECB encrypts each block independently with the same key, so repeated content shows up as repeated ciphertext, revealing structure. AES itself is fine; the mode is the problem. Use an authenticated mode such as GCM.

questions.question: Complete the function so password reset tokens are unpredictable.
choices: random.randbytes
secrets.token_urlsafe
random.getrandbits
secrets.randbelow
questions.explanation: secrets.token_urlsafe(32) returns 32 bytes from the operating system's secure random source, encoded for URLs. The random module is predictable once an attacker sees enough output, and secrets.randbelow(32) returns a number below 32, only 32 possibilities.
